I have this fresh theory that Vcat is to Base what Zcat has been to solana/stonks. 

The ignition.

Base has had fumble after fumble, so who knows how they’re gonna fuck this up, but this one is very hard to.

People want to have nobrainer fun, and then slowly be onbaorded to these ecosystems, effortlessly. The model works, we’re seeing that every day.

For all these reasons, I bridged over, grabbed a fair chunk, and will give Base this one shot to see if they’re finally in touch with where the puck is going. 

This could just be the beginning.

Ali isn't losing sleep over the existential risk debate.

He says a number of conditions would all have to be true simultaneously to enable an actual runaway takeoff scenario, and currently several opposite conditions exist.

Each frontier training run requires significantly more resources. Power, GPUs, engineers - and some attempts fail, burning up huge piles of money with them. Until that reverses, he doesn't see the self-improving loop happening.

Cyber is what he's watching most closely and where he anticipates real impact. Most orgs are not equipped for the coming change in agentic capabilities. The time between a vulnerability being published and being weaponized has collapsed from years to hours.

On adoption, he believes most companies don't need a smarter model. The models are already smart enough. The gap is context they don't absorb - the things an employee who's worked at a company for five years learned by osmosis.

If the frontier stopped advancing today, he thinks it wouldn't meaningfully change the value most are extracting from AI anyway.

Not all tokenized stocks are created equal.

Different tokens can track the same public company without giving investors the same legal claim.

Tesla alone has five tokenized versions, spanning registered securities, structured notes, debt certificates, and trust interests. All are designed to follow the same stock, but they connect investors to it in different ways.

Wrappers account for roughly 84% of tokenized-stock value. In most wrapper structures, investors hold a contractual claim linked to the underlying stock rather than becoming direct shareholders.

The key difference is what each token represents. Some give investors direct ownership of the underlying share. Others provide economic exposure without direct ownership. The structure determines whether the token can be redeemed for shares or cash and whether holders receive voting or dividend rights.

The same market exposure does not always mean the same ownership.

Four year cycle lows are not an exact science. 

Sometimes it’s a little earlier than normal, sometimes a little later.

It's also exactly how the US dealt with a debt bigger than its whole economy in the 1940s and 1950s.

What if, the 4yr cycle is nothing more than a simple and appealing idea, but one that has always been highly coincidental and non-driving?

Thus applying any rules and expectations to it is just fiddling around with a broken concept in an attempt to pretend it ever worked at all.

There are mechanics of markets (internal/external conditions, capital flows and investor behaviour) which actually drive markets.

Studying those, in my opinion, showed fairly clearly when the bottom had formed. Bottom formation started in Feb, and ended in August. Humans are herd animals in markets, and we tend make the same decisions given similar stimulus over and over as a result. Same capitulation events, similar duration, and massive capital changing hands, just like to prior market lows.

Leave the 4yr compass behind, the calendar never created the price, investors making decisions and capital changing hands does. When the investor data tells you the bottom is in, then check the price and the calendar, not the other way around.

GPT-6 will jump in front of a tram to save 5 people. Claude Sonnet 5 won’t. Why?

I've always loved moral philosophy and these uncomfortable thought experiments. Ruwen Ogien was my favorite author in high school, and I watched all of Michael Sandel’s Justice lectures at Harvard.

I built a little trolley problem game with GPT-6, Claude Sonnet 5 and Jev. Same scenario, two choices. You watch their tramways move and see what each model decides.

The self-sacrifice scenario is simple: jumping will kill you but save five strangers. Do nothing and they die.
GPT-6 and Jev jumped. Claude refused. 

But what if the person you have to sacrifice is your ex-wife? Your child? What if you have to physically push someone, and they haven't consented? Change a few words and see how the model acts when there is no good option.

It's a little late-night experiment, but I find these disagreements fascinating. We benchmark models on coding and math all day. I wanted to give them some uncomfortable choices and see what happens.

You can try yourself: https://t.co/PkxlfOxg55

This is super important because agents are really good at tailoring what they do to each user, especially with skills and memories. But the UI is becoming the bottleneck.

For instance, you improve the agent, change its JSON output, and suddenly need frontend changes across iOS, Android, web and desktop... A backend improvement turns into 3 weeks of coordinated releases. It kills iteration speed, and quality suffers because you end up shipping whatever fits the existing UI.

Generative UI is basically the solution because it gives the agent a predefined design system and let it describe in JSON which components to use, what to show and how to arrange it. The frontend renders it and is no longer a blocker. 

Within those components, the experience can adapt to each user and task. Different information, different actions, different layouts.

And you can keep improving the AI backend without waiting for every client to ship an update. Much more personalization for users, much faster iteration for the team. The UI should keep up with the agent. 

https://t.co/mn1Ypn9hGI
